articles.title: Berlin mapped 900,000 street trees. Now 12,000 people water them.
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Amanda Gläser-Bligh named her street tree Linda. Linda is a linden, eight years old, growing outside Gläser-Bligh’s apartment building in Charlottenburg, and once a week during Berlin’s hot months, Gläser-Bligh makes a couple of trips up and down the stairs with a watering can until she has carried 20 […]
The post Berlin mapped 900,000 street trees. Now 12,000 people water them. first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
Image alt text: A volunteer using the Gieß den Kiez app to water an adopted street tree in Berlin during a summer heatwave

Amanda Gläser-Bligh has named her street tree Linda. Linda is a linden, eight years old, growing outside Gläser-Bligh’s apartment building in Charlottenburg, and once a week during Berlin’s hot months, Gläser-Bligh makes a couple of trips up and down the stairs with a watering can until she has carried 20 liters (about five gallons) of water to Linda’s roots. Passersby sometimes stop and stare. They usually end up asking what she’s doing, and most of them, once they find out, look up at the tree a little differently.

Berlin has nearly a million street trees, and like cities across Europe, it’s watching them struggle through increasingly hot summers. A project called Gieß den Kiez, which translates to “water your neighborhood” in German, is trying to close the gap between what the city’s maintenance crews can do and what the trees need, by giving ordinary people a map, a reason, and a social framework for showing up with a watering can. Twelve thousand people have signed up.

900,000 trees color-coded by thirst and updated in real time

Developed by CityLAB Berlin, the Gieß den Kiez app tracks more than 900,000 trees across the city and calculates each tree’s water needs based on its age, species, and local rainfall. Color-coding shows which trees are in critical condition. Saplings, which lack the deep root networks of mature trees, need more frequent watering to survive and are flagged accordingly. Volunteers can log a watering, see when a tree was last watered by someone else, and find the locations of Berlin’s public water pumps.

What separates it from other urban tree maps is real-time coordination. The 12,000 registered volunteers work alongside district maintenance crews who are already watering thousands of trees but can’t keep up when temperatures spike. On June 27, when Berlin recorded an all-time high of 39.9 degrees Celsius (103.8 degrees Fahrenheit), people poured 8,000 liters (roughly 2,100 gallons) of water over trees across the city in a single day.

Berliners are caring about trees like they care about pets

Anna Mehrländer, who has been leading the project for more than a year, expected to find that people cared about trees. She didn’t expect the intensity. “I was really surprised at just how deeply people care about trees — for many people it’s almost like caring for a pet,” she says.

The project launched in 2020, at the start of the Covid lockdowns, and the timing mattered more than anyone anticipated. The single biggest annual peak in waterings, nearly half a million liters, came in those early pandemic months. Mehrländer thinks people seized on the activity as a reason to go outside and reconnect with neighbors at a moment when ordinary social structures had fallen away. “Climate change is happening on our doorsteps,” she says. “But watering a tree is a small action that helps your neighbourhood cope as summers get hotter. It also creates community at a time when people are increasingly working from home and on their phones all day.”

Gläser-Bligh describes the experience as almost playful. “It feels very fun, almost like a video game,” she says. She’s also noticed that people who see her watering often discover they could do the same and simply hadn’t known they were allowed to. “Many people may want to water the trees, but they might feel weird about doing it or they’re not sure if it’s their responsibility. But if you have this app encouraging you, you know it’s the right thing to do.” The app is doing something alongside the map: giving people the social cover to act on an impulse they already had.

It’s about “critical infrastructure,” not aesthetics

Urban forestry expert Dr. Cecil Konijnendijk has proposed what he calls the 3:30:300 rule for city greening: every resident should be able to see at least three trees from their home, live in a neighborhood with 30 percent tree canopy cover, and be no more than 300 meters (about 985 feet) from a park or green space. Most cities fall well short, and it matters more than it used to.

Studies show trees cool the air during heatwaves, break up urban heat islands, reduce flooding risk, cut air pollution, and improve mental health outcomes. “In the past, trees were thought of as a nice aesthetic element in cities,” Konijnendijk says. “But now we’re starting to see them as critical infrastructure.” Which makes the trees already in the ground the most urgent priority. It takes 30 to 40 years before a new tree starts delivering the full ecosystem services of a mature one. The ones wilting through summer droughts right now are not replaceable on any useful timeline. Konijnendijk also points to soil sensors and lidar-based canopy scanning as tools for monitoring tree health at scale, with cities like Malmö and Singapore already using them.

The open-source offer

Because the code is open-source, any city can adapt it. Residents in Potsdam, Leipzig, Magdeburg, and the 17th arrondissement of Paris have already built their own versions. “Anyone can copy the code and set up their own Gieß den Kiez,” Mehrländer says. “The main requirement is a data set of all the trees in your city. It’s possible to replicate anywhere, from China to the UK.”

The platform needs two things: city tree data, which most urban administrations already have in some form, and people willing to show up with a watering can. If Berlin’s numbers are any guide, the second one isn’t usually the problem.
articles.source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

articles.title: UK bluefin tuna comeback shows nature can recover, says WWF
articles.summary: The tuna is one of several wildlife recoveries highlighted in a major new report from WWF.
articles.content:
Bluefin tuna have returned in huge numbers off the British coast after almost disappearing from UK waters.

The return of the giant predatory fish is one of several wildlife recoveries highlighted in a major new report from WWF, which it says shows conservation can work.

However, the Living Planet Report 2026 also found that monitored wildlife populations around the world have fallen by an average of 73% since 1970.

The wildlife conservation charity said nature remains in "freefall" but it called the report one of hope.

"It's not too late," Mike Barrett, chief scientific adviser at WWF-UK, told the BBC.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant positive environmental event: the recovery of bluefin tuna populations off the UK coast, demonstrating that conservation efforts can lead to tangible wildlife recoveries. This has broad significance for biodiversity and environmental health, supported by a major WWF report, providing sufficient context and hopeful implications for nature conservation.
articles.personality_title: Bluefin tuna make a strong comeback off UK coast, WWF report shows
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Bluefin tuna, a large and important fish species, had nearly disappeared from waters around the UK because of overfishing and other problems. Wildlife populations worldwide have dropped a lot since 1970, raising concerns about the health of nature.

**What happened** – Recently, bluefin tuna have returned in large numbers near the British coast. This comeback was highlighted in WWF’s Living Planet Report 2026, which celebrates this and other wildlife recoveries as proof that efforts to protect nature can work.

**Impact** – The return of bluefin tuna shows that with the right actions, endangered animals can recover even after serious declines. This example gives clear evidence that conservation programs can help restore important species and improve the environment.

**What’s next step** – Conservation groups and governments will likely continue working to protect bluefin tuna and other species. The report encourages ongoing efforts to stop wildlife decline and support nature’s recovery.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The strong return of bluefin tuna off the UK coast proves that nature can recover when people protect it carefully.

articles.title: Woody ‘blankets’ are being deployed on Arctic permafrost to reduce carbon emissions
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 08 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03045-8A start-up company is testing whether stabilizing areas of rapidly eroding permafrost can prevent greenhouse-gas emissions.
articles.content:
As permafrost thaws in the Arctic, a company wants to use blankets to prevent erosion of the landscape.Credit: Jeff Vanuga/Nature Photo Library/Science Photo Library

A Canadian start-up firm is developing a way to prevent greenhouse-gas emissions from permafrost by stabilizing the soil with an insulating ‘blanket’ of woody materials. If the method works, it could be the first tool to directly forestall green-house gas emissions that are escaping from permafrost as the Arctic heats.

“Our goal is to make sure the carbon in the soil remains buried,” says Cansu Culha, co-founder of PermaC and a natural-hazards researcher at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, Canada.

Earth’s frozen environments are thawing as temperatures rise in response to human emissions. The only reliable way to slow that melting on a global scale is to slash emissions from the burning of fossil fuels. But some researchers are exploring methods to prevent the thaw directly, ranging from placing reflective mats on glaciers to pumping water onto sea ice to thicken it.

Researchers say that PermaC’s approach is the first they know of to focus on preventing permafrost thaw and its associated emissions, which are estimated to be equivalent to those of Japan.

The company just completed the first test of its insulating blankets in Canada’s Northwest Territories at an area of rapidly eroding permafrost known as a retrogressive thaw slump. These slumps occur when a hill of permafrost thaws and collapses, enabling erosion to take big bites out of the landscape. This exposes deeper layers of soil to warming, forming hotspots of CO 2 and methane emissions. One estimate suggests that these areas of rapid erosion could amplify permafrost emissions by as much as 40% compared to models that only account for gradual thaw.

The company’s approach is to stabilize the edge of the slumps with a layer of wood shavings, soil and native seeds, and a burlap-like mat of coconut husks. Culha says she got the idea after hearing about Indigenous communities in Alaska that prevent permafrost degradation by planting trees along the edges of slumps. Similar erosion-control blankets are used in temperate areas, but they haven’t been used to insulate or stabilize permafrost until now, she says.

PermaC has yet to release results from this year'stest. But the blanket seems to have halted erosion: over the Arctic summer, the edge of the slump without the blanket retreated by 5 metres, whereas the blanketed area saw no measurable retreat, Culha says.

“That’s very promising,” says Christina Schaedel, a permafrost scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Falmouth, Massachusetts, who has been advising the company. However, the result is from only one slump over one summer, she adds.

Green blanket

One challenge is calculating how much CO 2 the blankets prevent from being emitted. Measuring the CO 2 emissions from slumps is not straightforward and remains an active research question, says Mark Lara, a biologist who studies permafrost landscapes at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. “There definitely are slumps that are spewing out carbon,” he says. But there are “lots of minutiae that could dramatically impact the results”, he adds. For instance, the emissions from any given slump depend on its geometry, the amount of carbon in the soil and how much of that carbon ends up as CO 2 or methane after erosion.

So far, Culha has only rough estimates for the emissions that the blankets might prevent. Extrapolating from research on erosion rates and soil carbon in the Arctic, she thinks that about 2,200 tonnes of CO 2 a year might be prevented from being emitted at the average carbon-rich slump. If those calculations are accurate and the blankets can be installed at 20,000 slumps across Canada and Alaska — the company’s ambitious goal over the next decade — she estimates that they might prevent about 40 million tonnes of CO 2 emissions a year, roughly equivalent to the annual emissions of Hungary.

Culha says the company is developing a detailed methodology that a third party could use to verify prevented emissions, which would be necessary for the company to sell carbon credits for emissions the blankets prevent. People could purchase those credits to offset emissions elsewhere. The firm aims to issue credits as soon as next year, and has so far raised Can$1.4 million (US$1 million) from investors, says Culha.

articles.personality_title: Canadian start-up tests woody blankets to protect Arctic permafrost and reduce emissions
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Permafrost is frozen soil found in the Arctic that contains large amounts of carbon. As the Earth warms, this permafrost thaws and releases greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide and methane, which contribute to climate change. Stopping this thaw is difficult, and few solutions exist to directly protect the permafrost.

**What happened** – A Canadian start-up called PermaC is trying an innovative approach to slow permafrost thaw. They cover areas of rapidly eroding permafrost with insulating blankets made from wood shavings, soil, native seeds, and coconut husk mats. This method was tested in Canada’s Northwest Territories during the summer of 2026. Early observations showed that areas covered by the blankets did not erode, while uncovered areas shrank by about 5 meters.

**Impact** – This is the first known method aimed specifically at stopping permafrost from thawing and releasing greenhouse gases. If successful, it could prevent large amounts of carbon from escaping into the atmosphere—potentially stopping millions of tonnes of emissions each year. This would help reduce the speed of climate change by tackling a problem that has no easy fix.

**What’s next step** – PermaC plans to develop a clear way to measure exactly how much carbon dioxide the blankets prevent from being released. This will allow them to sell carbon credits, which companies or people can buy to offset their own emissions. The company hopes to expand the use of these blankets to thousands of sites across Canada and Alaska over the next ten years.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A Canadian company is testing woody blankets to protect thawing Arctic permafrost, aiming to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by stabilizing the soil and slowing erosion.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une start-up canadienne teste des couvertures en bois pour protéger le pergélisol arctique et réduire les émissions
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le pergélisol est un sol gelé présent dans l’Arctique qui contient beaucoup de carbone. Avec le réchauffement de la Terre, ce pergélisol fond et libère des gaz à effet de serre comme le dioxyde de carbone et le méthane, ce qui accélère le changement climatique. Empêcher cette fonte est difficile, et il existe peu de solutions pour protéger directement le pergélisol.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une start-up canadienne appelée PermaC essaie une méthode innovante pour ralentir la fonte du pergélisol. Elle couvre les zones où le pergélisol s’érode rapidement avec des couvertures isolantes faites de copeaux de bois, de terre, de graines locales et de nattes de fibres de noix de coco. Cette méthode a été testée dans les Territoires du Nord-Ouest du Canada durant l’été 2026. Les premières observations montrent que les zones couvertes par les couvertures ne se sont pas érodées, tandis que les zones découvertes ont reculé d’environ 5 mètres.

**Impact** – C’est la première méthode connue visant spécifiquement à empêcher le pergélisol de fondre et de libérer des gaz à effet de serre. Si elle réussit, elle pourrait empêcher la libération de grandes quantités de carbone dans l’atmosphère, évitant ainsi des millions de tonnes d’émissions chaque année. Cela aiderait à ralentir le changement climatique en s’attaquant à un problème difficile à résoudre.

**Prochaine étape** – PermaC prévoit de développer une méthode claire pour mesurer exactement combien de dioxyde de carbone les couvertures empêchent de s’échapper. Cela leur permettra de vendre des crédits carbone, que les entreprises ou les particuliers pourront acheter pour compenser leurs propres émissions. La société espère étendre l’utilisation de ces couvertures à des milliers de sites au Canada et en Alaska dans les dix prochaines années.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Une entreprise canadienne teste des couvertures en bois pour protéger le pergélisol arctique en train de fondre, afin de réduire les émissions de gaz à effet de serre en stabilisant le sol et en ralentissant l’érosion.
articles.personality_title_es: Una start-up canadiense prueba mantas de madera para proteger el permafrost ártico y reducir emisiones
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El permafrost es un suelo congelado que se encuentra en el Ártico y que contiene grandes cantidades de carbono. A medida que la Tierra se calienta, este permafrost se derrite y libera gases de efecto invernadero como dióxido de carbono y metano, que aceleran el cambio climático. Detener este derretimiento es difícil y existen pocas soluciones para proteger directamente el permafrost.

**Qué pasó** – Una start-up canadiense llamada PermaC está probando un método innovador para frenar el derretimiento del permafrost. Cubren áreas donde el permafrost se está erosionando rápidamente con mantas aislantes hechas de virutas de madera, tierra, semillas nativas y esteras de cáscara de coco. Este método se probó en los Territorios del Noroeste de Canadá durante el verano de 2026. Las primeras observaciones mostraron que las áreas cubiertas con las mantas no se erosionaron, mientras que las áreas descubiertas retrocedieron unos 5 metros.

**Impacto** – Esta es la primera técnica conocida que se enfoca directamente en evitar que el permafrost se derrita y libere gases de efecto invernadero. Si tiene éxito, podría evitar que grandes cantidades de carbono escapen a la atmósfera, deteniendo millones de toneladas de emisiones cada año. Esto ayudaría a reducir la velocidad del cambio climático al atacar un problema difícil de resolver.

**Próximo paso** – PermaC planea desarrollar una forma clara de medir cuánto dióxido de carbono evitan que se libere las mantas. Esto les permitirá vender créditos de carbono, que empresas o personas podrán comprar para compensar sus propias emisiones. La empresa espera expandir el uso de estas mantas a miles de sitios en Canadá y Alaska en los próximos diez años.

**Resumen en una frase** – Una empresa canadiense está probando mantas de madera para proteger el permafrost ártico que se está derritiendo, con el objetivo de reducir las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero al estabilizar el suelo y frenar la erosión.

articles.title: London’s Oxford Street gets fully pedestrianized this month: here’s what that means

The post London’s Oxford Street gets fully pedestrianized this month: here’s what that means first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
Image alt text: Pedestrians walking along a traffic-free section of Oxford Street in London following the October 2026 pedestrianization announcement

Oxford Street, one of the busiest shopping streets in the world, goes traffic-free on October 26. London Mayor Sadiq Khan announced the closure of the stretch from Orchard Street to Great Portland Street, nearly a kilometer (just under half a mile) through the heart of the West End, to all vehicles: buses, taxis, bikes, everything. Khan has been promising this for years. Now there’s a date.

“The transformation of the nation’s high street into a pedestrian plaza will begin in earnest,” Khan said, describing a future with flagship retail alongside cultural events and “next-generation workplaces.”

What the change looks like on the ground

October 26 is a first phase. New seating and other street-level changes are being installed as temporary fixtures so data can be collected before anything permanent is decided. Transport for London and the Oxford Street Development Corporation are handling the safety measures and rerouting logistics. The full length of Oxford Street, which runs well beyond this initial stretch, is still in play for later phases.

This has been fought over for a long time. Plans to pedestrianize Oxford Street have circulated through multiple mayoral administrations, stalling repeatedly in negotiations with Westminster City Council, which governs the area and has consistently pushed back. It’s still pushing back.

The objections, and which ones have substance

Westminster City Council deputy leader Tim Barnes said the council still has “a long list of unanswered questions about how it will work.” His main concern is traffic displacement: vehicles that currently move through Oxford Street will be rerouted somewhere, and Barnes says that somewhere is the smaller residential and commercial streets nearby. He called the timeline rushed and said the council is writing to the Oxford Street Development Corporation with formal concerns. The council also recently accused Khan of bypassing the need for a full environmental impact assessment, which the mayor and the government both dispute.

The displacement concern is the one with a real answer needed. Pedestrianization moves cars; it doesn’t eliminate them. Evidence from other cities shows that congestion on nearby streets does go up during the transition, sometimes significantly, before driving habits adjust. Whether the benefits to the main street outweigh those side effects over time is what the data from this phase is supposed to resolve.

Cities that did it first

Copenhagen removed cars from Strøget, its main shopping street, in 1962. Retailers predicted lost business. Foot traffic went up instead. New York pedestrianized Times Square in 2009, and retail performance in the area improved in the years that followed. Madrid and Oslo have both substantially reduced car access to their city centers in recent years, with similar results on foot traffic and air quality. The pattern is consistent enough that the debate about whether pedestrianization works in principle is largely settled. The debate is about this specific street, this specific transition, and who carries the cost while it sorts itself out.

Oxford Street draws around 300,000 visitors a day. Come October 26, the road they walk along will be theirs. Whether that changes their experience enough to justify taking the rest of the street is the question the next few months are designed to answer.

articles.personality_title: London’s Oxford Street closes to traffic to create a pedestrian-friendly space
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Oxford Street in London is one of the busiest shopping streets in the world, attracting about 300,000 visitors a day. For years, there have been plans to make part of it car-free to improve the area for shoppers and residents.

**What happened** – Starting October 26, a nearly one-kilometer section of Oxford Street, from Orchard Street to Great Portland Street, will be closed to all vehicles including buses, taxis, and bikes. This first phase will introduce temporary seating and street changes to test how the area works without traffic. The city’s transport team will collect data before making permanent decisions.

**Impact** – This change aims to create a safer, cleaner, and more pleasant space for pedestrians. Other cities like Copenhagen and New York have done similar projects and saw more visitors and better business. However, some nearby local leaders worry that traffic will just move to smaller streets, causing congestion there. The next few months will show if the benefits on Oxford Street outweigh these challenges.

**What’s next step** – Officials will study how the area performs with the new pedestrian zone. Depending on the results, they may extend car-free zones further along Oxford Street or make permanent changes. They will also need to address concerns about traffic moving into neighboring streets.

**One-sentence takeaway** – London is starting to transform a busy shopping street into a traffic-free space to improve safety and air quality, with careful testing planned before permanent changes.
articles.personality_title_fr: La rue Oxford de Londres devient piétonne pour créer un espace sans voitures
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La rue Oxford à Londres est l’une des rues commerçantes les plus fréquentées au monde, avec environ 300 000 visiteurs par jour. Depuis des années, des projets visent à rendre une partie de cette rue sans voitures pour améliorer l’espace pour les piétons et les riverains.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – À partir du 26 octobre, une section d’environ un kilomètre de la rue Oxford, entre Orchard Street et Great Portland Street, sera fermée à tous les véhicules, y compris les bus, taxis et vélos. Cette première phase introduira des sièges temporaires et des aménagements pour tester le fonctionnement sans trafic. Les responsables collecteront des données avant de décider des changements définitifs.

**Impact** – Ce changement vise à créer un espace plus sûr, plus propre et plus agréable pour les piétons. D’autres villes comme Copenhague et New York ont mené des projets similaires et ont constaté une augmentation des visiteurs et des commerces. Cependant, certains élus locaux craignent que la circulation ne se déplace vers les petites rues voisines, provoquant des embouteillages. Les prochains mois permettront de voir si les avantages pour la rue Oxford compensent ces difficultés.

**Prochaine étape** – Les autorités étudieront les effets de cette zone piétonne. Selon les résultats, elles pourraient étendre les zones sans voitures dans d’autres parties de la rue Oxford ou faire des aménagements permanents. Elles devront aussi gérer les inquiétudes liées au déplacement du trafic vers les rues voisines.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Londres commence à transformer une rue commerçante très fréquentée en espace sans voitures pour améliorer la sécurité et la qualité de l’air, avec des tests avant des changements définitifs.
articles.personality_title_es: Oxford Street de Londres se cierra al tráfico para crear un espacio peatonal
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Oxford Street en Londres es una de las calles comerciales más concurridas del mundo, con alrededor de 300,000 visitantes diarios. Desde hace años, se han planeado proyectos para hacer que una parte sea libre de coches y mejorar el espacio para peatones y vecinos.

**Qué pasó** – A partir del 26 de octubre, casi un kilómetro de Oxford Street, desde Orchard Street hasta Great Portland Street, estará cerrado a todos los vehículos, incluidos autobuses, taxis y bicicletas. Esta primera fase incluirá asientos temporales y cambios en la calle para probar cómo funciona sin tráfico. Los responsables recogerán datos antes de tomar decisiones permanentes.

**Impacto** – Este cambio busca crear un espacio más seguro, limpio y agradable para los peatones. Otras ciudades como Copenhague y Nueva York han hecho proyectos similares y han visto aumentar visitantes y negocios. Sin embargo, algunos líderes locales temen que el tráfico se desplace a calles pequeñas cercanas, causando congestionamiento. Los próximos meses mostrarán si los beneficios en Oxford Street superan estos problemas.

**Próximo paso** – Las autoridades evaluarán cómo funciona la zona peatonal. Según los resultados, podrían ampliar las zonas sin coches en Oxford Street o hacer cambios permanentes. También deberán resolver las preocupaciones sobre el tráfico que se traslade a calles vecinas.

**Resumen en una frase** – Londres comienza a transformar una calle comercial muy concurrida en un espacio sin tráfico para mejorar la seguridad y la calidad del aire, con pruebas antes de cambios permanentes.
